summary: This note is the body of a Journal of Monetary Economics article by Cristiano Cantore and Lukas B. Freund (2021) on fiscal policy and household heterogeneity. It proposes a tractable two-agent New Keynesian model in which 'workers' face portfolio adjustment costs on bond holdings and 'capitalists' own all firms but do not supply labor. The authors argue this matches micro-data iMPCs and avoids implausible profit income effects on labor supply, yielding smaller fiscal multipliers than the traditional two-agent (TANK-UH) model. The excerpt ends mid-section on the worker household's interest-rate elasticity and forward guidance.
one_line: A 2021 Journal of Monetary Economics paper proposing a tractable capitalist-worker two-agent New Keynesian model to study fiscal policy and household heterogeneity.
key_facts: The article is 'Workers, capitalists, and the government: fiscal policy and income (re)distribution' by Cristiano Cantore and Lukas B. Freund, published in Journal of Monetary Economics, Volume 119, April 2021, pages 58-74.

The paper proposes a two-agent New Keynesian model in which workers can save in bonds subject to portfolio adjustment costs, while firm ownership is concentrated among capitalists who do not supply labor.
The model's capitalist-worker structure ensures that transmission of demand shocks under sticky prices does not rely on income effects on labor supply induced by countercyclical markups.
Relative to the traditional two-agent model, the paper finds fiscal multipliers are smaller and the sensitivity of the output path to public deficits is dampened.
The traditional two-agent model is called TANK-UH (unconstrained and hand-to-mouth households); the new model is called TANK-CW (capitalist and worker).
Fagereng et al. (2018) estimated household consumption responses to lottery winnings using Norwegian administrative data; the quarterly point estimate for the iMPC is approximately 0.2.
Cumulatively over the first four quarters after the shock, the average household in the Fagereng et al. (2018) estimates consumes around half of the windfall.

Auclert et al. (2018, p.17) diagnose: 'Due to the absence of intermediately constrained agents, [the traditional two-agent model] cannot generate elevated iMPCs in year one and later, which are a key characteristic of the data.'

Proposition 1 states that the worker household's impact consumption response to an unanticipated one-off income windfall is given by equation (6), and for hand-to-mouth limiting case the worker's response reduces to that of a hand-to-mouth household.
Portfolio adjustment costs are quadratic, scaled by steady-state income, and rebated to workers as a lump sum that workers do not take into account when making savings decisions.
The paper's log-linearization is around a steady state with zero inflation, no government spending or debt, and total output normalized to unity.
The traditional two-agent model is built on Galí et al. (2007) and Bilbiie (2008), with Rotemberg quadratic price adjustment costs and a Taylor rule for monetary policy.
The paper's JEL classification codes are E12, E21, E25, E32, and E62.
The authors state that two-agent models are tractable laboratories and not competitors to HANK models such as Kaplan et al. (2018) or Hagedorn et al. (2019b).
